title: Peace, be still (Mark 4:35–41)
hook: reading the storm again: why are you fearful

segments.voice: Yesterday, the seed that grows while you sleep, automatē, of itself. Your line was it grows while you sleep. Did you leave something to grow on its own? Today, the same evening, out on the lake. Day two hundred three.

We've met this storm before, back in the stories. Now we're reading Mark in order, and you can see where it falls: at the end of the same long day of parables. Jesus has been teaching from a boat. Evening comes, and he says, let's cross to the other side. They push off, just as they are. Then a great storm of wind rises, the waves beat into the boat, and it starts filling with water. Some of these men are fishermen. They know what a filling boat means. Today's word: peace.
screen: `THE SAME LONG DAY.` → `LET US CROSS OVER.` → `A SUDDEN STORM.`

segments.voice: First, the sleeper. Mark gives a small, human detail. In the Douay-Rheims: "And he was in the hinder part of the ship, sleeping upon a pillow; and they awake him, and say to him: Master, doth it not concern thee that we perish?" A cushion in the stern. Asleep, after a day of teaching. And the disciples don't only ask for help. They ask, don't you care? It's a question, not just a plea. Second, the command. He gets up and rebukes the wind and says to the sea: "Peace, be still." In Mark's Greek, be still is literally be muzzled, the same word he used when Jesus silenced a demon in Capernaum. The wind stops, and there's a great calm. Third, the question to them. "Why are you fearful? have you not faith yet?" Not yet. Mark's disciples are slow learners, and he doesn't hide it. Fourth, their question. Now they're more afraid than they were in the storm, and they say to each other: "Who is this (thinkest thou) that both wind and sea obey him?" Here's why that question matters, and why we just spent five weeks in the Psalms. In the psalms, it's God who rules the sea and stills its waves; one psalm tells of God turning a storm into a breeze. So when the wind obeys Jesus, the disciples are left staring at a question the psalms seem to answer. Mark doesn't answer it for them yet. He lets it hang there, in a quiet boat, in the dark. This week began with sins forgiven, and it ends with the sea obeying. Who is this?
screen: `ASLEEP ON A CUSHION.` · `PEACE, BE MUZZLED.` · `HAVE YOU NOT FAITH YET?` · `IN THE PSALMS, GOD RULES THE SEA.` · then, large: `WHO IS THIS THAT BOTH WIND AND SEA OBEY HIM?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name the storm and say the words. Settle, and breathe. What's the storm this week? Name it plainly: the bill, the diagnosis, the argument, the fear that wakes you. Picture it as wind and water in a small boat. Now, if you pray, say the words into it, slowly: peace, be still. You can say them as a prayer to Christ. If you don't pray, say them to yourself, to your own racing mind, and let your breath slow. The bell holds the time.
Peace. The first word Jesus speaks to the storm: peace, be still. And the calm that leaves the disciples asking who he is. Today's word.

Your line: who is this. This week: sins first, the sabbath, the twelve, a widened family, the sower, the sleeping seed, the storm. Today, when something calms that you thought wouldn't, ask the disciples' question. Day two hundred three.

howItsDone: Catholics hear the calming of the storm at Sunday Mass in Ordinary Time; Pope Francis preached on this passage in an empty St. Peter's Square during the COVID-19 pandemic.

what a scholar hears: pephimōso, be muzzled, the verb of the Capernaum exorcism; Psalm 106 [107] has God still the storm.
